newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Close Brothers targets fee earners.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Close Brothers targets fee earners.

text.p: UK investment bank Close Brothers Group Plc aims to increase its fee earning business over the coming years, its chief executive Rod Kent said on Monday.
"We want to increase the fee earning businesses," Kent told Reuters in a telephone interview following the announcement of record results for the financial year to the end of July.
These saw Close Brothers increase pretax profits by 33 percent to 45.1 million stg, from 34.0 million the year before.
Kent said the main fee earners the group was targeting were corporate finance activity and investment management.
In June Close Brothers bought Hill Samuel's corporate finance division. Kent said the new business had "got off to a marvellous start" and had retained both staff and clients.

He cited a recent Hambro Company Guide which listed Close Brothers as top financial adviser in the "fastest growing clients" category. It was second in the "clients with fastest increasing earnings" division.
Close Brothers' new-look corporate finance team was ranked fifth based on the number of stock market clients it advised.
"This transaction has really put us on the map in the corporate finance area," Kent added.
Kent said the group wanted to grow its investment management business, having already built up a range of services.
"We would like to be relatively bigger," he said. This growth would either come through buying businesses or organically by taking on the right personnel.

"The question is finding the right companies and the right people," Kent said, adding that given that the stock market was at all time highs it was not the best time to go out and buy and investment management business.
Commenting on the year's results, Kent said he was happy with the overall performance of the group.
He said the group had reached agreement to sell its loss-making U.S. venture and was not planning to make any other overseas forays in the immediate future.
"We are not against international business, but the right thing has to come along. We have looked at several European markets but for one reason or another they have not been right," he added.

A 17 percent increase in the group's total dividend, to 10.0 pence from 8.5 pence the previous year, was "a pretty bullish signal" Kent said, adding that earnings per share had risen by only 12 percent because of a rights issue in the first half.
Close Brothers' lending business had performed extremely well over the year, Kent said. Both volumes and margins were up over the period, he added.

Winterflood Securities, the group's market-making operation, had a record year as a result of a bouyant stock market. Kent said the business could cope with any market changes, although the division's profits were always likely to fluctuate.
